title: Black bream (sooty grunter)

names.note: Dictionary: 'black bream', with no note on fresh or salt water. See the Names section for which fish this is.

identification.basis: The dictionary gives only the English 'black bream'. In north Queensland fresh water, 'black bream' is the everyday name of the sooty grunter (Hephaestus fuliginosus), and Roth used 'black bream' in 1901 for a fish of the river snags alongside barramundi. At Bloomfield the estuarine pikey bream (Acanthopagrus pacificus) is a second candidate, so speakers should confirm. The fish called black bream on the Mitchell at Karma Waters is the sooty grunter.

summary: **Barrbal** is the Kuku Yalanji dictionary word for 'black bream' [ref:hershberger1982]. In the fresh water of north Queensland, black bream is the **sooty grunter** (*Hephaestus fuliginosus*), a thick-lipped, sooty-black fish of rocky pools and snags [ref:wp-sooty] [ref:nfa-sooty]. It is the black bream that [Karma Waters Station](place:karma-waters) shows off from its stretch of the Mitchell River [ref:karma-camping]. Kuku Yalanji people fished the freshwater creeks with bark [lines](entry:hooks-and-lines) and [lawyer-cane](entry:lawyer-cane) thorn hooks, [speared](entry:spear-and-woomera) in clear water and used [plant poisons](entry:fish-poisoning) in the late dry season [ref:anderson1996]. Their inland neighbours on the Palmer used bone-barbed hooks and two-person [nets](entry:nets) [ref:roth1901]. In Queensland today a sooty grunter must be **at least 28 cm**, and there is a combined limit of 10 grunter [ref:qld-fresh].

sections.heading: Names
sections.body:
The dictionary gives **barrbal** 'black bream' [ref:hershberger1982]. It does not say whether the fish lives in fresh or salt water, so the English name has to be read the way north Queenslanders use it.

**Why this page treats barrbal as the sooty grunter.** In north Queensland fresh water, 'black bream' is the usual name for *Hephaestus fuliginosus* [ref:wp-sooty] [ref:nfa-sooty]. Roth used the name the same way in 1901, for a big fish that lay with [barramundi](entry:barramundi) among the snags of the lower Tully River [ref:roth1901]. On the Mitchell at [Karma Waters](place:karma-waters) the black bream is this fish [ref:karma-camping].

**The Bloomfield doubt.** The dictionary was made with Bloomfield River speakers [ref:hershberger1982], and the Bloomfield estuaries also hold the **pikey bream** (*Acanthopagrus pacificus*), a true sea bream. The Atlas of Living Australia has records of pikey bream, sooty grunter and khaki grunter within 25 km of the Bloomfield River mouth [ref:ala]. Anderson lists 'various species of bream' among the fish taken with [hook and line](entry:hooks-and-lines) on the Bloomfield coast [ref:anderson1996]. If an elder from Wujal Wujal uses barrbal for the estuary bream, that is their word to settle.

**Grunters.** Two more dictionary words, **jarbir** and **kurriyala**, are both glossed 'species of fish, grunter' [ref:hershberger1982]. *Kurriyala* is also the word for the carpet snake. Several fish called grunter live around Bloomfield, among them the silver, khaki, crescent and sooty grunters [ref:ala]. Which fish each word names is not recorded. Bloomfield fishermen used a small grunter as bait [ref:anderson1996].

sections.heading: Description
sections.body: A deep-bodied, thick-lipped fish, brownish-grey to **sooty black** with darker scale margins. Some have golden blotches on the sides [ref:wp-sooty]. Most are about 25 cm and 400 g, but they can reach 54 cm and 6.2 kg [ref:wp-sooty] [ref:nfa-sooty]. Sooty grunter eat almost anything: shrimp, worms, insects, frogs, algae, plant roots and **palm berries** [ref:nfa-sooty]. They are tough fish that put up with clear or muddy water, still or flowing, and a wide range of temperatures [ref:wp-sooty].

sections.heading: Where it lives
sections.body:
Sooty grunter live in freshwater streams from Cape Hillsborough north along the Queensland east coast, through Cape York and the Gulf of Carpentaria rivers, and west to the Daly River in the Northern Territory [ref:nfa-sooty]. They like flowing water over rock, and lurk around rocks, sunken logs and in pools below waterfalls [ref:wp-sooty].

**Karma Waters and the upper Mitchell.** The Atlas of Living Australia holds sooty grunter records from the upper Mitchell country dated 2008 to 2026, including one about 25 km east-south-east of the [Karma Waters](place:karma-waters) homestead. It also has records of a close relative, the coal grunter (*Hephaestus carbo*), near Mount Carbine [ref:ala]. The station's own camping page features the black bream of its river [ref:karma-camping]. Fish the rocky runs, the heads of pools and the snags.

sections.heading: Seasons
sections.body:
Sooty grunter spawn in **summer**, as the rivers rise with the monsoon, sometimes in groups [ref:wp-sooty]. Spawning starts once the water is warmer than 25 °C, and schools of up to 50 fish have been seen spawning together in water less than half a metre deep [ref:nfa-sooty].

The dry season was the main freshwater fishing time. The dictionary's bark [nets](entry:nets) were 'dragged through the water in the dry season when the water goes down' [ref:hershberger1982]. Inland at Bloomfield, [fish poisons](entry:fish-poisoning) were a late-dry method, used when the smaller creeks broke up into separate waterholes [ref:anderson1996]. Roth found [bush fences](entry:fish-traps) built only in flood time, to catch the bigger fish going back downstream [ref:roth1901].

sections.heading: Uses
sections.body:
Barrbal is a food fish. Anglers rate the sooty grunter 'fair to good eating, with a slightly weedy flavour' [ref:nfa-sooty]. The Kuku Yalanji freshwater kit, recorded by Anderson at Bloomfield [ref:anderson1996], was:

- **[Lines](entry:hooks-and-lines)** of *Sterculia quadrifolia* bark with **hooks made from [lawyer-cane](entry:lawyer-cane) thorns**, used in freshwater creeks and waterholes for [turtle](entry:freshwater-turtle), [eelfish](entry:eels), [catfish](entry:catfish) and perch. Bait was grubs, [small freshwater prawns](entry:cherabin) or small frogs. Line fishing was mostly women's work.
- **[Spears](entry:spear-and-woomera)**, which worked only in fairly clear water, thrown with the *balur*, a short spear thrower made for fishing.
- **[Plant poisons](entry:fish-poisoning)** in the late dry season.

The dictionary adds *badur* 'hook and line', *mandurr* 'bait (any kind)', *makarr* '[fish net](entry:nets)' and [*miyil*](entry:fish-poison-plants), a tree whose sap was 'used to blind fish' [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: How it was caught and cooked
sections.body:
**[Hook and line](entry:hooks-and-lines) in fresh water (Bloomfield Kuku Yalanji)** [ref:anderson1996]:

1. Twist a line from the bark of *Sterculia quadrifolia*.
2. Make the hook from a **[lawyer-cane](entry:lawyer-cane) thorn**.
3. Bait it with a grub, a [small freshwater prawn](entry:cherabin) or a small frog.
4. Hold the line in the hand, or tie it to a stick pushed into the bank.

**The Palmer River hook (Koko-minni).** The hook had a **wooden shank with a bone barb** of kangaroo bone or a [catfish](entry:catfish) spine [ref:roth1901].

**Spearing among the snags (lower Tully River, Mallanpara country).** For [barramundi](entry:barramundi) and black bream lying among the snags, men **crept up very quietly, or dived**, and struck the fish **from the side or from underneath** [ref:roth1901]. In deep or muddy waterholes, where the fish can't be seen, men struck here and there on the chance of a hit [ref:roth1901].

**Two-person [nets](entry:nets) (Palmer and Laura).** On the Palmer the net was made of *Acacia leptocarpa* [string](entry:string-and-twine) on a large oval frame [ref:roth1901]:

1. Two people carry the framed net upright through the water.
2. Friends in front act as beaters and drive the fish towards it.
3. The net is lifted as soon as a fish is in.

Roth recorded that the Koko-yellanji of the Laura called this net *jikan-ikan* (his 1901 spelling).

**Grass fence (the Peninsula generally).** In a shallow waterhole, the women of the camp lined up side by side across the hole. They moved forward on hands and knees, pushing thick bundles of grass and leafy boughs ahead of them, and drove the fish onto the bank [ref:roth1901].

**[Fish poison](entry:fish-poisoning) (late dry, inland Bloomfield)** [ref:anderson1996]:

1. Choose a waterhole that has been cut off as the creek dries.
2. Smash [*Erythrophleum chlorostachys*](entry:ironwood) bark and leaves under water, or swirl a grass sponge holding mashed [*Barringtonia*](entry:fish-poison-plants) seed or stem.
3. Collect the stunned fish as they float up. Divers kept their eyes shut tight and did not swim through the poison.
4. The hole could not be used again until a storm and flood renewed the water.

On the middle Palmer the Koko-minni threw in the bark of *Adenanthera abrosperma*, or leaves of *Careya* or *Eucalyptus resinifera*, leaving the leaves for one to three days. Edward Palmer recorded *Barringtonia racemosa* and *Luffa* used on the Mitchell River [ref:roth1901].

**Killing and cooking.** Kill a fish by **biting deeply just behind the head**, so it can't flip back into the water [ref:roth1901]. Roast it on the coals (*dindal*) [ref:hershberger1982], or bake it in the [earth oven](entry:earth-oven) (*kurrma*) lined with wild-ginger leaves [ref:roth1901].

sections.heading: Safety
sections.body:
The Mitchell at Karma Waters is [freshwater crocodile](entry:freshwater-crocodile) water [ref:karma-camping]. Freshies are usually shy, but a big one can give a serious bite [ref:am-johnstoni]. [Saltwater crocodiles](entry:saltwater-crocodile) do travel, so follow the Crocwise fishing rules: **stand back from the edge, cut a snagged line rather than wading in, and never clean fish at the water's edge** [ref:crocwise].

The [fish poisons](entry:fish-poisoning) above are real poisons. *Miyil* sap can blind [ref:hershberger1982]. They are recorded here as history, not as methods to use.

sections.heading: On Country today
sections.body:
**Recreational rules (Queensland fresh water).** A sooty grunter must be **at least 28 cm**. There is a **combined limit of 10** for Gulf, khaki, lake and sooty grunter [ref:qld-fresh]. In fresh water you may use up to **6 lines, each with one hook or lure**, and up to 4 traps of the permitted kinds. You may **not** use a spear or spear gun, a cast net or a seine net [ref:qld-gear]. If you're fishing the Mitchell in October, remember that **[barramundi](entry:barramundi) are closed in Gulf fresh waters from 7 October to 31 January**, and you can't target them even for catch-and-release [ref:qld-closed].

**Native title.** The 2013 Western Yalanji determinations recognise rights to **hunt, fish and gather on the land and waters for personal, domestic and non-commercial communal purposes** [ref:brady2013]. A further Western Yalanji determination followed in August 2026 [ref:nit2026wy]. Under section 211 of the *Native Title Act 1993*, native title holders fishing for those needs do not need the licences and permits other people need [ref:alrc]. [Karma Waters](place:karma-waters)' agreement with the Western Yalanji Traditional Owners was the first on pastoral land in Australia [ref:karma]. Guests should follow the station's induction and rules, and ask Traditional Owners before fishing elsewhere on their country.

**At Karma Waters.** Karma Waters Station falls under the earlier 1998 *Western Yalanji or 'Sunset' Peoples v Pedersen* consent determination, the first consent determination of native title over a pastoral property in Australia [ref:wyac2020] [ref:kw-about]. See the [Karma Waters guide](/dictionaries/kuku_yalanji/country/places/karma-waters) for what it covers, and ask the Traditional Owners and the station before hunting, fishing or gathering.

sections.heading: Language
sections.body: *kuyu* 'fish'; *mala-kuyu* 'good fisherman'; *badur* '[hook and line](entry:hooks-and-lines)'; *mandurr* 'bait (any kind)'; *mungkil* 'spear to kill', as in *Bula minya wali-yindu walu-yindu kalkabu mungkin* 'They speared lots of different kinds of fish'; *yijirr* 'fish scales'; *jijirr* 'red bream' [ref:hershberger1982].
